item.content:encoded:
Tibetan woman stages fresh protest in Lhasa, demands justice for imprisoned brother Dorje Tashi According to Phayul, Gonpo Kyi has been leading a sustained campaign for her brother’s release and judicial review for several years. Her efforts have included solo demonstrations, sit-ins, prayer vigils and hunger strikes outside government offices, police stations and courts in Lhasa. Representative image (File photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Tibetan woman Gonpo Kyi staged another peaceful protest outside the High People’s Court of the so-called Tibet Autonomous Region (TAR) in Lhasa on October 26, demanding justice for her imprisoned brother, Dorje Tashi, according to a report by Phayul. A newly surfaced video circulating on X (formerly Twitter) reportedly shows Gonpo Kyi protesting outside the court, seeking a review of her brother’s life sentence, a retrial and permission to visit him in prison. According to Phayul, Gonpo Kyi has been leading a sustained campaign for her brother’s release and judicial review for several years. Her efforts have included solo demonstrations, sit-ins, prayer vigils and hunger strikes outside government offices, police stations and courts in Lhasa. Dorje Tashi, once a prominent Tibetan businessman, was arrested in the aftermath of the 2008 protests in occupied Tibet. He was reportedly subjected to months of torture while in detention. In 2010, following a closed-door trial at the Lhasa Intermediate People’s Court, he was sentenced to life imprisonment on charges of loan fraud. However, his supporters have maintained that the charges were politically motivated. His brother, Dorje Tseten, was sentenced to six years in prison in the same case and was subsequently released. Phayul reported that Dorje Tashi’s family has repeatedly pursued judicial review through various legal channels since his imprisonment. In 2020, Chinese authorities rejected appeals filed by his lawyer and relatives seeking reconsideration of his conviction. Between 2023 and 2024, Gonpo Kyi, her husband Choekyong and her brother Dorje Tseten reportedly staged more than seven hunger strikes and prayer protests outside government offices and courts in Lhasa, demanding a review of the life sentence and permission for family visits. The report also highlighted alleged repeated physical assaults, police beatings, interrogations and both short- and long-term detentions faced by Gonpo Kyi and her family in connection with their campaign. On August 20, 2025, Gonpo Kyi reportedly jumped from the second floor of the Yak Hotel in Lhasa in an apparent suicide attempt after being denied permission to visit her brother and allegedly placed under hotel arrest. She sustained serious injuries and was left in critical condition. The case has also attracted international attention, with both the United States and the European Union raising concerns over Dorje Tashi’s imprisonment. According to Phayul, during the 51st session of the UN Human Rights Council, held from September 12 to October 7, 2022, the European Union called for the immediate and unconditional release of several individuals, including Dorje Tashi. The US Department of State also documented Dorje Tashi’s detention in its 2021 and 2022 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices on China, highlighting his case in its assessment of human rights conditions in the country. (ANI)

item.title: Iranian Navy says it destroyed "enemy submarine" and damaged two oil tankers near Strait of Hormuz
item.description: "This morning, an enemy submarine that was operating in the operational area east of the Strait of Hormuz was hit and destroyed by Iranian Navy sailors," the Navy statement said.
item.content:encoded:
Iranian Navy says it destroyed "enemy submarine" and damaged two oil tankers near Strait of Hormuz "This morning, an enemy submarine that was operating in the operational area east of the Strait of Hormuz was hit and destroyed by Iranian Navy sailors," the Navy statement said. ANI | Updated: 30-10-2026 18:35 IST | Created: 30-10-2026 18:35 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Iran

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Iranian naval forces destroyed an "enemy submarine" and damaged two commercial oil tankers in the operational zone east of the strategic Strait of Hormuz on Friday morning. State media Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) reported, citing the Iranian Navy's Public Relations department, that Iranian forces targeted and destroyed an adversary submarine navigating the operational sector near the vital maritime choke point. "This morning, an enemy submarine that was operating in the operational area east of the Strait of Hormuz was hit and destroyed by Iranian Navy sailors," the Navy statement said. In a separate development, state broadcasters reported that two oil tankers caught fire in the same maritime zone after striking sea mines. Iranian officials attributed the incident to the vessels ignoring official maritime safety warnings and operating covertly. "Two enemy tankers, which, regardless of the warnings and regulations announced, were travelling in prohibited and unsafe areas east of the Strait of Hormuz with their tracking systems turned off, were damaged and caught fire after hitting naval mines," the statement added. Iranian naval authorities explicitly placed the blame for the incident on the commercial operators, asserting through IRIB that vessel owners would be held accountable for navigating unauthorised routes. "The tanker owners will bear full responsibility for the consequences of unauthorised traffic and disregard for safety and maritime warnings," the statement warned. Reiterating a strict security posture over the regional waterways, the Iranian Armed Forces issued a direct warning against any unauthorised presence or military probing near Iranian territorial interests. "We warn the enemy that any movement, infiltration, or provocative action in areas under the supervision of the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran will be met with a strong and proportionate response," the statement concluded. The incident comes amid heightened tensions over maritime traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian military authorities asserting control over the waterway and warning commercial vessels against transiting through areas they consider restricted and unsafe. Iran's Army Navy Public Relations, in a statement reported by state broadcaster IRIB, claimed that a tanker travelling in a restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz had caught fire after striking a naval mine."This morning, a tanker travelling in a restricted and unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz was damaged and caught fire after hitting a naval mine, preventing it from moving," the statement said. Iranian naval authorities also warned vessels against attempting uncoordinated passage through the waterway, stating, "The Strait of Hormuz is closed to violating ships that intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas without coordination and relying on the lies of the US President."Senior Iranian military officials have also reiterated that the waterway would remain closed until Tehran's conditions were met. "The Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Iran's conditions are met, under the control of the warriors of Islam," Major General Yazidi said, according to IRIB. The developments come as Washington weighs its military and diplomatic options regarding Iran. The Wall Street Journal reported that the head of the US military's Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on military options for Iran during a White House meeting on Thursday. The meeting was also attended by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman General Dan Caine and other Cabinet members, the newspaper reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the discussions. The deliberations come amid reports of a possible resumption of major US combat operations against Iran, following the US-Israeli bombing campaign earlier this year on February 28. Washington has also increased air defences, munitions and other supplies across the Middle East in recent weeks, according to the report. (ANI)

item.title: INSIGHT-Trump touted a record Venezuela oil deal. Now reality is setting in
item.description: By Marianna Parraga, Mircely Guanipa and Mariela Nava HOUSTON/MARACAIBO, Venezuela, Oct 30 (Reuters) - P resident Donald Trump called it the biggest oil deal in history: 17 Ven ...
item.content:encoded:
INSIGHT-Trump touted a record Venezuela oil deal. Now reality is setting in Reuters | Updated: 30-10-2026 15:31 IST | Created: 30-10-2026 15:31 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

By Marianna Parraga, Mircely Guanipa and Mariela Nava HOUSTON/MARACAIBO, Venezuela, Oct 30 (Reuters) - P resident Donald Trump called it the biggest oil deal in history: 17 Venezuelan oilfields holding some 64 billion barrels of reserves, handed to a single company. Delivering on it falls to North American Blue Energy Partners, a little-known firm led by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who was until recently a target of US money-laundering investigations involving funds embezzled from the state-owned oil company PDVSA. The company's deal with Washington grants the US a 35%-stake in its corporate parent and the right to buy 20% of output at production cost. NABEP says it will lift oil output fourfold to more than 1 million barrels per day (bpd), up from about 224,000 bpd in mid-October. That will be far harder than Trump and NABEP have suggested, according to Reuters interviews with 15 oil workers, contractors, financiers and industry experts. Eight of them — seven oilfield workers and contractors and one business associate familiar with NABEP operations — said the company was carrying debt to contractors and struggling to hire staff and repair infrastructure. Even the headline reserves figures Trump cites may overstate the prize. Only about 10 billion barrels can realistically be developed within the 25-year term Venezuelan law allows for oil projects, Francisco Monaldi, director of the Latin America Energy Program at Rice University's Baker Institute, told Reuters. "And only if everything aligns," he said. Terry Wade, a spokesperson for NABEP, told Reuters the company was on track. "We're at the leading edge of a Venezuelan oil industry renaissance," he said. NABEP faces a steep set of challenges, the industry players said. The company must secure capital; compete for rigs, equipment and power plants; execute a long list of repairs to dilapidated infrastructure; and rapidly increase its workforce in a country that has seen a decades-long exodus of trained staff. Former Venezuelan energy minister Humberto Calderon Berti told a conference in September he was convinced "the agreement will not last long," citing the company's lack of technical qualifications and short track record. Once owned by an asphalt tycoon, NABEP entered Venezuela's energy sector in 2024 with three projects under contracts with Nicolas Maduro, the former president who was ousted by US military forces in January. It took operational control of 14 more fields on October 1 under agreements with the Venezuelan government that it said included production targets. The company has relied on local contractors to hire staff, procure equipment and make routine operating decisions, according to the oilfield workers and contractors and the business associate. Three of the workers and the associate said NABEP owes money to some of those business partners. Reuters could not determine the amount of debt. Wade said NABEP's supplier base is expanding while it migrates to a new payment system. "All invoices are being paid, and any disruption will be addressed," he said. The company, which is not publicly traded, says it has invested $1 billion of its own capital since 2024 and would increase the amount it re-invests each year by as much as 50% to meet its targets. Venezuela's oil ministry and state-owned PDVSA did not reply to requests for comment. Interim President Delcy Rodriguez has defended the pact. PDVSA's Vice President Jovanny Martinez told state media this week that NABEP could meet its 1 million bpd target in six to seven years. But about 80% of roughly 4,000 inactive wells in the Maracaibo basin, one of the regions where the company operates, need repair. The country's overall crude output has remained stagnant in recent months at about 1.2 million bpd, according to official figures. Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela this week, told reporters in Caracas on Thursday that she had not seen the NABEP contract, but that it fell short on transparency. "Of course we want investment. The issue is how and with whom," she said. White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said: "Production is growing and this deal is already delivering results for the American people." NABEP says it employs about 5,000 people directly and more than 10,000 contractors. The company has hired administrative employees from PDVSA in recent weeks, three people with knowledge of its recruiting said. It is rushing to hire technical staff and field workers needed to expand, they added. BIG TARGETS, NEW RIGS Oil output is expected to rise at Junin Sur in the Orinoco Belt, where NABEP's expansion is mainly focused. But gains at the highly polluted, aging Maracaibo basin will likely take longer. At Petrozamora, three workers described idle heavy machinery, damaged facilities, oil leaks and delayed payments from NABEP to suppliers. Wade said Petrozamora was implementing an improvement plan, and NABEP had installed new equipment on Lake Maracaibo. Betancourt, on a tour in Petrozamora last week, said output there had reached 115,000 bpd, up from 98,000 in September, according to PDVSA internal data. He offered no long-term targets. Satellite analysis from a Venezuela-focused intelligence firm in early October found no drilling infrastructure at seven of the 17 fields. Junin Sur had one rig, and drilling equipment from a previous operator remained at Lake Maracaibo. NABEP says it has lined up 60 rigs and 70 pieces of heavy machinery to arrive in batches. Drone footage and photos it provided from the second half of October showed rigs and a well cluster in Junin Sur, and a drilling barge in Lake Maracaibo. The company said three drilling rigs were working at Orinoco and three more would be added soon. It said it also has 13 workover rigs, which are used to repair and prepare existing wells, and is waiting for 15 more refurbished and fully inspected rigs. Six of NABEP's new areas are virgin territory, far from roads or oil infrastructure, adding to the challenge of boosting production. FUNDING AND REPUTATION HURDLES NABEP will need strong partners and massive funding, a banker involved in energy project financing and debt restructuring in Venezuela said. The company says it plans to develop the 17 large oilfields simultaneously. Such a task would be a challenge even for oil majors such as Chevron, ExxonMobil or ConocoPhillips, five industry experts told Reuters. Three people said NABEP has struggled to open bank accounts after US and European investigations into Betancourt's past dealings with the Venezuelan government. Betancourt has been investigated in the US in connection with an alleged plan that involved embezzling over $1 billion from Venezuela's PDVSA. That investigation was paused this year. The businessman has also been under investigation in Switzerland for money-laundering. He has never been charged with a crime in any jurisdiction. Wade said the company has access to foreign banks, without elaborating. NABEP may also find a challenge in partnering with Washington. When the first crude cargo under the deal reached Texas on Tuesday, Trump called the 1 million barrels a "gift." A White House official said the government had received it at no cost. NABEP initially said the oil was delivered under Washington's right to buy a portion of the company's production at cost. It later said it gave the shipment to the US at no cost to US taxpayer "to recognize the historic nature of the agreement." It was a telling start: NABEP may be pumping the oil, but Washington seems to be calling the shots. "To the victor belongs the spoils, right?" Trump said at the port of Corpus Christi on his way to an election rally.
